chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the woman whose husband divorces her, when does she become free to dispose of herself (i.e., complete her waiting period)? He said: When she sees the blood of the third menstruation, she is free to dispose of herself. I said: And if the blood comes early for her before the days of her menses? He said: If the blood is before ten days, it is considered hers (as a second menstruation), and it is from the menstruation from which she purified herself. And if the blood is after the ten days, it is from the third menstruation, so she is free to dispose of herself.

key_terms.أَمْلَكَ بِنَفْسِهَا: Free to dispose of herself (independence from husband's guardianship)

ai.seo_question: When does a divorced woman's waiting period end according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's chain clarifies the mechanism of 'talaq al-sughra' (revocable divorce) by defining the transition from marital guardianship to full independence based on the third menstrual cycle. It introduces a critical jurisprudential nuance: bleeding within the first ten days is treated as residual from the previous cycle, whereas bleeding after ten days constitutes a new menstruation, thereby completing the iddah. This distinction highlights the Shia emphasis on physiological markers in determining legal status, ensuring the woman's autonomy is restored only after the definitive third cycle is confirmed.
